subsubtopic: NUCLEAR TESTING-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 43, in view of the obvious imminence of tomorrow's five-megaton blast, and in light of the recent events involving the excavation of a second hole on Amchitka Island for a possible further detonation of a nuclear device, and because of the announced atmospheric nuclear explosion by the government of France and the likelihood of other countries continuing their own tests, I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):
That the government of Canada immediately request the Secretary General of the United Nations to immediately declare a one-year moratorium on all nuclear tests, so that the United Nations during that period might complete a permanent agreement to end all nuclear testing.
In view of earlier representations by this House and the nature of the motion, I feel the House might be disposed to pass the motion without debate and I urge the House to do so.

POSSIBLE U.S. EXCISE TAX ON AUTOMOBILES IMPORTED FROM CANADA, INCREASE IN SURTAX AND IMPLEMENTATION OF DISC-CANADIAN COUNTER-MEASURES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Finance. In light of the decision of the United States Senate finance committee to authorize additional powers to the President with regard to the imposition of an excise tax on automobiles imported from Canada and an additional surcharge, as well as its recommendations regarding DISC, could the minister now expand upon his statement yesterday that the Canadian government could be in a position to take appropriate counter-measures in the event that such action might be taken by the government of the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: POSSIBLE U.S. EXCISE TAX ON AUTOMOBILES IMPORTED FROM CANADA, INCREASE IN SURTAX AND IMPLEMENTATION OF DISC-CANADIAN COUNTER-MEASURES
speechtext: First of all, Mr. Speaker, I think it very unlikely that the President will take action with regard to changing the level of the surtax or imposing an excise tax. As a matter of fact, the United States administration have indicated several times that they would like to get rid of the surtax as soon as possible when stability of world currencies can be established and some other trading guidelines given. However, if they were to take such action we could take action in respect of taxes very quickly in this House. Of more concern to the government is the DISC program which was recommended in an amended form by a committee of the Senate. Of course this proposal has to go to a joint meeting of the two committees of the House of Representatives and the Senate and then the legislation has to go through both chambers. However, we are watching very closely to see what kind of DISC proposal ultimately comes out, if one does emerge from these consultations between the two Houses, and are considering what action we would take in that case.

subtopic: POSSIBLE U.S. EXCISE TAX ON AUTOMOBILES IMPORTED FROM CANADA, INCREASE IN SURTAX AND IMPLEMENTATION OF DISC-CANADIAN COUNTER-MEASURES
speechtext: Does the minister agree that this is a dangerous escalation, and is the Canadian government taking further initiatives both in regard to this move and also with regard to settling the international exchange situation which seems to underly the whole problem of the surcharge and our relationship with the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: POSSIBLE U.S. EXCISE TAX ON AUTOMOBILES IMPORTED FROM CANADA, INCREASE IN SURTAX AND IMPLEMENTATION OF DISC-CANADIAN COUNTER-MEASURES
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I do not consider it an escalation. They have simply granted authority to the President. In the United States the President has to have underlying authority in order that he may take action, whereas in Canada action on taxation under any circumstances can be taken by an announcement in this place. With respect to the DISC program, the announcement would indicate that it is in a much modified form from the form put forward by the administration, but if passed as recommended by the Senate committee it would still be very damaging to Canada, and we have protested officially with regard to the DISC program.
With regard to the underlying situation, talks took place in Ottawa yesterday and there will be further meetings. The next meeting of the Group of Ten is to be held later this month in Rome.

This is one of the sections that can be readily missed by a taxpayer because, notwithstanding the fact that in certain areas or certain sections of the bill stated expenses are allowed to be deducted, this is the little door right down in that back corner which gives the assessor a way to disallow deductions by simply quoting the following:
In computing income, no deduction shall be made in respect of an outlay or expense in respect of which any amount is otherwise deductible under this Act, except to the extent that the outlay or expense was reasonable in the circumstances.
This provision gives the assessor a straight discretion and it leads in so many instances to the biggest hassle between the taxpayer and the assessor. The parliamentary secretary might wish to consult the Minister of National Revenue as to where the balance lies. Perhaps the assistant deputy minister in the Finance Department who deals with taxation could also say from his experience in the tax field where the balance lies. I know that you can make a statute so rigid that you cannot get a break from the assessor now and then. On the other hand, what I do not like to see are funk holes whereby a taxpayer reading a section wherein it is stated that he shall be allowed certain expenses in relation to earned income, and then when he makes his claim, finds that under section 67 the assessor says "I do not think the expenses are reasonable under the circumstances".
We all know that if there is a serious question about an item it can go further up the line, and ultimately to a court. This is one of those sections under which neither the Tax Review Board nor the Federal Court of Appeals would substitute their discretion for that of the assessors. They will say it is not a matter of law. The Tax Review Board might, however, but certainly no member of what had been the Exchequer Court, and which will now be the appropriate division of the Federal Court, will substitute the court's discretion for that of the assessor which, by the time the case gets to the court, is the opinion of the minister. Who says they are not reasonable under the circumstances? These statutes cannot be written merely for administrative convenience. This is one point where I will stop, right there and then, if the criterion is to be always the administrative advantage. The taxpayer has a
November 5, 1971

tough enough fight as it is without our loading the dice against him all the time. This is one of those sections that, if it were in a contract, would be in superfine print. I want to get a full explanation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member noted, this does continue a provision that is in the present act. It is basically to provide that an outlay or an expense is deductible only to the extent that it is reasonable.
Why don't you say so?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The words "in respect of which any amount is otherwise deductible," that appear in this section are there to make it clear that the limit also applies where the deduction is indirect rather than direct. An example of that might be where a person paid an exorbitant amount of money for a capital asset, which he then depreciates, and the depreciation, an indirect deduction from income in this sense, would have to be reasonable and be related to a reasonable capital cost.
On the basic question of jurisprudence, Mr. Chairman, I can only say that I do not think the courts have ever been particularly shy in accepting the responsibility of determining what is or is not reasonable. It is a mixed question of law and fact. Usually, when it comes under a taxing statute more often it is a question of fact, and they will exercise their jurisdiction and discretion in determining whether the taxpayer has been reasonable and perhaps whether the tax assessor has been unreasonable in his interpretation of the transaction.

I hate to disagree with the parliamentary secretary's opinion, but if there is an indication that there is an appeal on a point of law to a particular court-and we must remember that in many instances on this point appeals only lie on a point of law- the matter of reasonable interpretation gets terribly short shrift on application to the court. This is what I am questioning all along the line. This is why I feel there are some difficulties here.
It would be better with respect to this question of reasonableness if a direct indication were given in bold letters in conjunction with the main section dealing with expenses, rather than having it tucked away in the position that I have described of being in very fine print. I say this because when we come to consider sections 66, 69 and so forth, the subject matters are entirely different.

If I have not correctly understood, then I am sure he will appreciate that my difficulty in following him lies in my being this far away from him in the chamber at the present time. Does the hon. member suggest that the present test of reasonableness for this type of expense should be replaced by some codified, arbitrarily defined one outlining the categories of expense? Is he suggesting that?

I should like to enter this discussion, Mr. Chairman. He put the roof back on the cottage and carried out repairs to bring it back to its former condition. These were held to be expenses properly incurred and reasonable in the circumstances to earned income. Being a sensible fellow, he decided that the next storm was not going to do that type of damage if it could be prevented. He extended and strengthened the retaining walls, taking an ounce of prevention to head off a ton of headaches. It was held by the courts that the retaining wall was a capital expense and was not reasonable in the circumstances for earning an income.

Paragraph (c) provides that the taxpayer's estate or the beneficiary are deemed to have acquired this property. Paragraph (d) covers the case where the estate of the beneficiary has acquired a particular depreciated asset. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, of course.

At the bottom of page 173 in subsection 6(b) an amendement was introduced the
Income Tax Act
other day to the effect that the taxpayer, the spouse and the trust had to reside in Canada. This was not a provision in the original instance but has now been introduced. Why is there this particular limitation in respect of the exemption, that all the parties and the trust must be resident in Canada simultaneously.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The underlined words in the amendment to this section have been added to provide that the rules set forth in the paragraph apply only where the taxpayer and the spouse or the trust are resident in Canada at the time of the taxpayer's death. Without this addition, the roll-over could apply to non-residents and that is not the normal way of handling transfer to non-residents.

If I may say so with respect, I am wondering why it is absolutely essential that all concerned must be residents of Canada at the time in order that there be a roll-over. I can think of cases where the husband, the taxpayer, is a non-resident but is the owner of property here in Canada. The devolution is to his spouse who is resident in Canada and the trust could be here in Canada. Why in such circumstances should the spouse be disentitled to the benefit of the roll-over? She is a Canadian resident in Canada. The trust is here in Canada and the property is here in Canada. He might happen to be resident somewhere else, perhaps for reasons of health or otherwise. The state says that it should not get into the bedrooms of the nation, so let us not become involved in an investigation, in respect of the Income Tax Act, concerning why the parties are not living together. The husband bequeaths the property to his wife who remains in Canada and sets up a trust with a Canadian executor or trust company. Here, we have a completely Canadian situation. But you say that in those circumstances they are tainted with some foreignness and therefore may not qualify. I do not understand it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think the hon. member has raised a set of circumstances which merit some looking into. Of course, the section is drawn with the idea that the property might roll-over out of Canada and thus be put beyond the writ of the Minister of National Revenue. However, I would be pleased to take a look at this particular set of facts which the hon. member has suggested in relation to this section. If indeed some change is indicated, we would be most pleased to bring it in at a later date.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the amendment carry?

Agreed.
Amendment (Mr. Gray) agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall section 70 as amended carry?

Agreed.
Clause 1, section 70 as amended agreed to.
Conditionally.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
We now have before us section 72. This section is amended and the text of the amendment is to be found at page 8940 of Hansard for October 22. Shall I read it?

November 5, 1971
Income Tax Act

Please do not read it.
On Clause 1-Section 72-Reserves, etc. for year of Death

Here again, Mr. Chairman, the same situation applies. I ask why must the transferor and the transferee be resident in Canada. Why must it be conjunctive, particularly if the transferee is resident in Canada and the property is in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, while the parliamentary secretary is pondering his reply to that very important point, could I also suggest, since this is a new provision, that we have a brief explanation for the record concerning why this is being proposed. I ask this because many people in an affluent society may leave very vast estates and perhaps not realize all the implications for those who will succeed to those estates.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this section provides a special rule for the taxation year in which the taxpayer dies. It denies him the deduction in respect of certain reserves that he would normally be permitted, but it also provides an exception to this special rule for property of this kind which he leaves to his spouse or to a trust for his spouse if she and his executors elect to take advantage of it. If they do, the general rule is that deductions shall be made in computing the taxpayer's income for the year in which he died and corresponding amounts included in the income of the spouse or the trust. The amendment provides that the special rule covering such items of income as accounts receivable and the business carried on by the taxpayer in the year he died will apply only if the taxpayer and the transferee are resident in Canada at the time of the taxpayer's death. It is not intended that the rule apply where one or the other or both are non-resident.

I am sorry, I may be a
little dense on this, but it seems to me that this section specifies when there shall be a denial of the setting up of the reserve. There is a denial of the setting up of the reserve. Why do you insist, in denying what you might say is a privilege to a taxpayer, that both the taxpayer and his wife be resident in Canada? I cannot understand the idea in this context of insisting that both be resident in Canada. Let us put the shoe on the other foot. The provision will not apply if either of the transferor or transferee is not resident in Canada, and presumably there would be an entitlement to a reserve.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The amendment does not go to the denial, it goes to the carrying forward, the election in the option, as I understand it. The amendment would come into play in section 72(2).

I may have to ask someone to give me a private briefing session because I still do not get it. The conclusion which the parliamentary secretary has indicated in this section or elsewhere is the greatest breach of logic and development in the whole of section 72. We start out in section 72 by setting up exclusions of reserves. Does he mean to tell me that we have switched to the other side of the medal and are now granting a right in that section?
[The Assistant Deputy Chairman.]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman.

Surely to goodness, something is going wrong in that kind of drafting. This only leads to confusion. I am looking at a section which I deem to be an enumeration of exclusions of reserves, and yet half way through we come to just the reverse. Is that the explanation? I think it is nonsensical.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Subsection (1) is the denial and subsection (2) is an exception to that denial. It seems to me that this is a rather logical place to put it. The continuity is there, and it is better to place it right there than elsewhere in the bill.

Now, the parliamentary secretary has said that this is an exception to the denial, but the exception to the denial seems to be based on the fact that both parties must be resident in Canada, so that if one of the parties is non-resident in Canada the exception would be granted.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, the denial of the right would apply if either or both parties are non-resident. That is the result.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the amendment carry?

Agreed.
Amendment (Mr. Gray) agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall section 72 as amended carry?

Agreed.
Clause 1, section 72, as amended, agreed to.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Now, we will go to section 74 as amended, and the text of that amendment will be found at page 8941 of Hansard for October 22.
On clause 1-Section 74: Transfers to Spouse.

I have two questions arising out of section 74. The first one is that while the side note on page 177 reads, "gain or loss deemed that of transferor", the fact is that there is no specific provision within the act dealing with loss, but certainly there is with regard to gain. So, I think we should have an explanation of this omission.
The other question concerns something which has not been changed at all, that is section 74(5) which I call the "Mama and Papa" clause. We have had at least some contributions to the debate in that regard, although not much of a change in the law which would help good old Mama and Papa. The section about which I am really curious is the old one. It is the last part of section 74(5) which reads:
Where a husband and wife were partners in a business, the income of one spouse from the business for a taxation year may, in the discretion of the Minister, be deemed to belong to the other spouse.
For curiosity's sake I went to the bible that I have been using, the Canadian Master Tax Guide, to see whether there was much litigation or disputation between government and taxpayer with regard to the Mama and Papa
November 5, 1971

section. I find that there is almost none, which suggests to me one thing, not that there is no room for improvement there but rather than the Mama and Papa type of business is apt to be run on such lines that there is not much profit from it, that Mama and Papa simply cannot afford the expensive litigation in the courts to determine their rights. I have made the point before that we have not made a proper examination of the provisions in the Income Tax Act relating to the small family business in this country operated by Mama and Papa as we have done in other areas.
When there are hundreds of millions of dollars involved, do we not all get excited in this parliament? But when there are cases of husbands and wives living on very submarginal incomes, operating small grocery stores, small garages or any small business that you would like to name, we simply have not given their problems close examination. I hope the parliamentary secretary will indicate that these provisions-admittedly we are dealing with piggy bank type operations-have received some examination by the department before we were presented with this large catalogue of tax changes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The first point with which the hon. member dealt was the marginal note. In the section as it is, and particularly as it will be amended, there is a netting out of gains and losses to arrive at this end, and I believe that is the explanation.
As to the other question, I believe it goes back to the general area which was covered before. I am afraid that no satisfactory solution to the matter of the Mamma and Papa store has been advanced. We are still in the position where, as the hon. member has noted, some hardship may indeed fall where the husband and wife relationship is in this context a bona fide business relationship.

Mr. Chairman, I want to take up the cudgels along with the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants to try to defeat this old rule that identifies as one a husband and wife participating in the same business, and which says that the spouse cannot be an employee of the other. The consequence of this provision will be that no child care allowance is claimable by the spouse if she has to go and work in her husband's business unless, of course, it is incorporated. This is where the nonsensical position comes about.
It may be a small business to which the total applicable tax rate might be 21 per cent, and for the individual paying on marginal rates this is not a very high income. But if the husband incorporates the corner grocery store, as the sole proprietor he may put a share in trust with his lawyer and that makes it a Limited company, but with no greater investment in it, except that now it has "Ltd." added to the name. The wife may now be hired as a clerk, and they may have to pay some unemployment insurance premiums for her. They will have to pay Canada Pension Plan contributions for her. That is one way in which they can be covered by the Canada Pension Plan. She in turn, will be able to claim the worker's allowance, and she would also be able to claim the child care allowance. But where there is no "Ltd." she will not get the child care allowance or worker's allowance. She is not able to con-
Income Tax Act
tribute to the Canada Pension Plan, and of course there would be no further point in paying insurance contributions on her behalf. That is the consequence of continuing section 74(3) in effect. And, of course, the same remarks apply to section 74(5), where the husband is a partner in a firm.
I have gone through this time and time again, yet there is a persistence on the government side in refusing to effect change, unless the store is incorporated. In fact, with a small business of that nature incorporation is a pure sham. I wonder why the government insists on the fiction and the sham of incorporation under these circumstances. I have heard it said that administratively it would be difficult for the Tax Department to keep track of these individuals if this change were made. That is founded on a lack of understanding of how much track the government does keep of individuals. It might have been valid 20 years ago, but today all the people involved here have social security numbers. If they file under unemployment insurance that will be another place where track of them will be kept. If they file under the Canada Pension Plan, that will be another place where track of them will be kept. And I am sure that we will see regulations with respect to worker's allowance and child care allowance. You can bet your bottom dollar that there will be regulations with respect to identification. Yet here, we persist in what I say is a nineteenth century concept of the relationship between taxpayer and spouse in matters of this kind.

Mr. Chairman, when the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants raised this question originally I participated in the debate, and the parliamentary secretary did explain why husband and wife were being treated this way. But, Mr. Chairman, there are many people affected. You only need to walk around this city and you will see many small food stores that remain open in the evening. Probably the wife opens the store at eight o'clock in the morning and runs it until noon, then her husband takes over and later their children help. These people are earning a livelihood by providing a service to the citizens. They are not going on relief. Businesses of this type are being operated in all towns and villages in Ontario and throughout this great dominion in which husbands and wives work as partners.
If the husband hires somebody else to do the work that his wife might do in the store, a deduction can be made for that as an expense. But for the life of me, I cannot understand why it is not possible for the husband to hire his own wife to work in the store and get a deduction for that. The wife contributes to the success of the business. He should have a right to make deductions for her wages in the same way he would if he were hiring somebody else to do the work. Can the parliamentary secretary explain why this has to be made so tangled, why a man cannot hire his wife, pay her wages, and charge them off to the business? Is there any particular, definite reason? Will it cost the national treasury a lot of money if we allow this? Is there any estimate of that cost?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the matter is purely one of trying to avoid leaving gaping loopholes in the law for people to take advantage of in order to avoid taxation. As I admitted in answering the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants, there is a hardship worked on husband and wife
November 5, 1971

Income Tax Act
situations where there is in fact a bona fide commercial relationship. However, so far no alternative has suggested itself that would allow us to resolve both problems satisfactorily, that is the one that the law, as it presently is, does resolve, plus the problem which hon. members have raised on two or three occasions during this debate.

Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary secretary talks about a gaping hole. Again I ask how much will it cost the treasury of Canada to allow what we are seeking? We are told that this bill is tax reform. We are asking for a minor change that could help small businessmen to be more successful. Why not make the change we suggest, and then see whether any loopholes appear? The parliamentary secretary cannot say there will be a gaping hole until we do this and see what happens. If one appears, it can be taken care of by an amendment to the Income Tax Act next year. This act can be amended next year if you find a lot of people are bilking the government out of taxes that it thought it was going to get.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is not a matter of revenue. It is a matter of equity, and the government simply does not see why small businessmen should be given the option of an income split when wage and salary earners are not going to have that option.

Mr. Chairman, sections 72, 73 and 74 are all intertwined, but they have to be considered individually. There is a tremendous mixup here, and that has been demonstrated to us by the parliamentary secretary. It is suggested that there is some loophole in the government's right to take everything we own. Surely, this is a complete reversal of logical thinking. Throughout the history of the British parliamentary system, the onus has been placed on governments to prove to the taxpayers why governments should take money from them. It is not a question of whether or not a taxpayer is taking advantage of a loophole, but a question of whether a government has justification for taking away the money that the taxpayer has earned. We have gone around in a complete circle when we say it is up to the taxpayer to prove in a court of law, or even in this chamber, that he has a right to escape taxation. It is true that once the law is there, he cannot avoid taxation. That is why it is incumbent upon us as the only voice of the taxpayer to make sure that the law with which the government intends to strangle the citizen does leave some outlet for his private enterprise.
.00 p.m.)
It seems to me that over the centuries the married woman has been a neglected person, a second-class citizen. There are many ways in which women's rights are shouted from the housetops today. We hear about abortions and equal pay, but here is something equally important-the right of a woman to help her husband earn a living. As I read this section, there is very little relief for the family type of project. We will talk about the family farm later; but today in many small businesses the little woman comes in from watching her children and runs the grocery store.
I take great exception to the fact that the government thinks it has some God-given right to take every cent from our citizens unless they can prove they do not have a right

to the money. They only have a right to it, apparently, when the Income Tax Act says they have. I shall fight to the best of my ability in order to see that the law of Canada never gets to the point where we take over all the means of production for the family farm and the family business to the point where the individual has no rights.
I am worried about the Carter report. I am worried about the government taking the view that because a royal commission was established to look into our taxation system and some well known egghead has proposed an answer to all our problems, we should bow down and worship the written word. True, we paid for that report- but the Carter report is not the law of the Medes and the Persians which alters not. It is our duty to alter it, to amend this act which nobody seems to understand. I am supposed to be trained in the law and I flatter myself that I am as subtle as most ordinary people, but I find it difficult to understand this bill. There is no security whatsoever for the housewife in the small, unincorporated business. She has no real rights under the Canada Pension Plan and if her husband were allowed to pay for her, the competition from the large corporations-for whom I have very little sympathy-the chain stores, the great combines, the international corporations which are as dangerous as some governments-
Oh, hardly.
Not quite, but nearly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Keep him on the party line, Jack.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I would expect the things I am saying to be said by any real Liberal. I suppose you could classify me as a left wing Conservative. There are no real Liberals in this country. I have not heard real liberalism coming from the other side of this House for the last 14 years.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Paul Hellyer is the only one.

I admit I am speaking Gladstone Liberalism. A square deal for the little people, not backed up by land and estates or large holdings in India, and foreign domination, that has all gone by the board. Let us not have the class war any more. In Canada an individual still has the right to earn a living and his wife has the right to help him. I am opposed to the many sections of this act which threaten that right.
Hear, hear!
I think we should expect the Liberal government to be the champions of the little people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We are.

I do not see it in this legislation. I do not see anything in this bill to protect the little businesses which are failing at the rate of some 3,000 a year. This cannot be blamed on the Leader of the Opposition because, if my memory serves me correctly, there has been a Liberal government in this country for five-sixths of the time.
Hear, hear!

Cheer-but the people of Canada have their eyes on you. You can beat on your desks, but they want to
November 5, 1971

know what you are going to do. This bill is not giving them the comfort and protection they deserve.
It takes a million people off the tax rolls.
Yes, and puts a million people on the unemployment rolls.
Oh, oh!

They would not be there but for the delinquency of your party. I would like to see you get to your feet and tell us what your plans are to give security to the small business people of this country. Mr. Chairman, may I have a little order?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I was going to call for order. I admit I cannot hear the hon. member.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: When you do hear him you might try and relate it to the bill.

I have been waiting for 14 years for these gentlemen to get to their feet and give us the benefit or some of their views. I would ask them for the courtesy of being heard for a few minutes in this chamber to see whether I have not some liberal views which they might adopt.
It is a very sad day for the people of Canada if their capital is to be diminished by taxation. This is one country where individuals still have some vestige of right to earn a living.
Hear, hear!

I beg hon. members in this chamber, through you, Mr. Chairman, to make sure that such a thing as good will which is built up through a lifetime of hard work is not taken away because of an unfair fiscal policy or a greedy government. I do not care how well thought-out are these plans for spending other people's money. I think there is still a place in Canada for leaving some small part of the income in the family.
I should like to have a better answer for taking it away than merely saying these individuals have found a loophole in the law. That is an insult to them. I want to know why any government can think it has a right to my private property. I am a free enterpriser, but whenever I have had a chance I have voted for the social security which is needed for our older people who have worked all their lives. Under this so-called free, democratic system they have a right to the benefits. I believe they are entitled to the old age pension and to fair prices on the farm and in the store that they helped to build up.
I see in the Carter report a sinister attempt to do legally things that the people of Canada do not want. That is the only reason why a document such as this would be presented to an unsuspecting public. It is obvious that members of this House do not understand the legislation, so how can we expect the taxpayer on the farm or in the small store to have any respect for us if we pass a bill which we do not understand ourselves.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is not the Carter report.

I agree that we have not gone as far in this bill as the Carter report, but we have gone as far as the
Income Tax Act
Canadian people will stomach. We have gone as far as we can bamboozle them, as far as can be crammed into 707 pages of closely written claptrap. This afternoon I asked a simple question, was a common law marriage a marriage, or was it not? I wanted an answer, yes or no. It is simple. Everybody understands what we are talking about. The answers I want are not to be found by perusing these sections.
Say a man starts out when he is 21 and spends all his life building up a family business. When he retired, will he, his wife or his children be allowed to benefit from that business, or will some greedy government take away what he has built up and say, "What we are doing is legal. Back in 1971 we gave you a chance to make your representations through your member. We amended the act. The benevolent government brought in 101 amendments in one afternoon." Mr. Chairman, merely because we do not pass them all in half an hour we are accused of filibustering.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, no.
And I am accused of being delinquent.
No, no.

Oh, yes, that is what it has come to. The delay will be said to be the fault of the Leader of the Opposition. It will be the fault of the opposition itself; all 70 members of the Official Opposition will be lumped together in this regard and 150-off members will say that they were held up because the Leader of the Opposition was not here to pass the bill for them. That is the sort of slippery attitude that we see exhibited on the other side of the House, and it is absolutely revolting for anybody who believes in the democratic process.
Filibustering will get you nowhere.
If the hon. member is having a hard time, why is his leader not here to help him?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member is having a hard time keeping to the amendment because of remarks from hon. members on the other side of the chamber. I wish hon. members would remain quiet.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, I am flattered by the attempts of the rabbits to get me off the bear tracks. I want some answers from the parliamentary secretary. A simple reading of this bill will not give me answers. The bill is not simple. The only thing that is simple and plain to understand is that: we are moving in on the free enterprise system. We are moving in on the family business unit and attempting to grind it down under the juggernaut wheels of Pharaoh.
If you introduce another four or five valuation days and another four five versions of the capital gains tax, you will destroy the whole free enterprise system of this country, as the Carter report suggested should be done. I have read the Carter report carefully and understand it, and it

November 5, 1971
Income Tax Act
recommends socialism by legislation. This is the old, creeping game of trying to do legally and by subterfuge what you know perfectly well the Canadian people do not want. The first thing done by parties that openly espouse socialism is to claim they are democrats. Yet what is democratic about expropriating all the small businesses in Canada? Whether you do it at the rate of 10 per cent a year now, 20 per cent per year in two years or 25 per cent per year in five years makes no difference.
What is the rationale behind taking away all private property in Canada and using it for the purposes the government may think are good? I do not happen to think those purposes are good. I think that a man knows better what he needs and what is good for him than any government, no matter how beneficial it may think it is. That is where I stand and those are the principles on which I was elected.
Oh, oh!

I hear boos and catcalls and talk about success. I suppose I have been successful in presenting the facts as I see them. As I say, I have no quarrel with the concept of social security and no quarrel with the taxing of large corporations which have made unconscionable profits. I find nothing wrong with that. There is nothing extremely socialistic about that. When companies pile up excess profits in our cities, by all means tax them.
If companies hold to ransom young people who want to build homes, and if those companies charge exorbitant rates, we should look at them, tax the excess profits and allow the treasury to use such money for purposes of sewage disposal and cleaning up the air. Use that money to clean up the environment. Take it away from the people who are openly robbing the families of this country of their just right to a lot 50 feet in frontage and 100 feet in depth on which they can build a home. That our young people are so robbed is a disgrace in this country. I think all governments should look at all sources of revenue, but they should not raise it by taxing exorbitantly the small businessman and making it impossible for him to allow his wife and children that degree of reasonable comfort which even people on relief and others who are contributing nothing to the welfare of the country are enjoying.
People will not be interested in free enterprise if they are so heavily taxed. People will not be interested in opening the small store and giving the kind of service which only a small store or business unit can give if after 40 years of hard work they are not able to take care of their children and if the widowed spouse cannot enjoy the benefits of that hard work. Taxes which will dissipate such property are to be levied. This is wrong. When the tax becomes due, the property must be disposed of immediately, within six months, and consideration must be given to deemed profits.
The government will not even give the family unit time to make any money because someone in the Department of National Revenue will say, "We think you ought to have made "X" dollars in a certain period." These people would expect the women or children to dispose of their property quickly and pay to a greedy government "X" dollars immediately or suffer the consequences. Why cannot the department wait until prices go up, say, or the

time for selling is better? But no, the people concerned must sell the property now. We want the same deal for everybody; no one should be dealt with overly severely.
Mr. Chairman, after reading this bill very carefully and after hearing what I heard this afternoon, I am not sure that if I were left, say, $10 million I would not go to Nassau and see if I could not escape some of these provisions. I know that many people in this country are earning good fees by helping others to evade some of these laws which are supposed to be foolproof.
People like lawyers.

Some people hire experts and accountants to help them evade the law, yet the small businessman who has built a family business must look ahead to the day when his family may have to sell the business.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.
Carry on.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Battle River.
Mr. Chairman, since this is a most important section, and since the remarks of the hon. member for Pembina have been most relevant, I think he ought to be allowed to continue.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I must ask the unanimous consent of the committee to do that. Is there such consent?
No.
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I believe the hon. member for Pembina may make further remarks because there were several interventions during his speech.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Yes. The Chair will recognize the hon. member for Pembina.

Mr. Chairman, I will not take up too much of the committee's time. If I have not made my point clear in the last few minutes, I will never make it clear. I hope it is clear. We should all take a good look at the principle behind the expropriating of family businesses. As I say, if I have not made my point understood in the last 15 minutes I do not think I could make it understood if I spoke for 15 hours on the subject. If I have not been understood, I am sorry and I feel sorry for the members of this chamber. It is a very, very important point and I am sure most hon. members know exactly what I am getting at. If they do not, I suggest that they read the Carter report again, thoroughly.
I admit that in the Carter report there are fine suggestions on how to stop those who are fleecing the Canadian people through escaping the payment of taxes due in legitimate fields of taxation. One of those taxation fields is that of excess profits. But when you get to the point of taxing every profit made, of taxing every benefit that
November 5, 1971

comes from free enterprise or family co-operation, I think you have reached the point of no return.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I bring to the attention of hon. members that we have had a very good debate this afternoon. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance has admitted that some important points have been raised. I hope the chief government whip will retract the press release in which he said that the House of Commons is no good, we have to do away with it and close it down. This report was contained in an article in the Citizen this afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, section 74(5) provides:
Where a husband and wife were partners in a business, the income of one spouse from the business for a taxation year may, in the discretion of the minister, be deemed to belong to the other spouse.
As with other taxation matters, the onus of proof lies on the individual taxpayer. This reminds me of a story that is going around. The Minister of Finance was driving along the highway in a big, black Cadillac. He was driving too fast and attracted the attention of an officer of the RCMP. The officer stopped the minister, went over to the big, black Cadillac and opened the door. Naturally, he was surprised to see the Minister of Finance. His only comment was "Oh, my God!" The Minister of Finance replied, "And don't you forget it."
Hear, hear!

Sections such as this, where something is at the discretion of the minister, amply bear this out. The hon. member for Pembina has very ably pointed out the troubles that can arise from sections such as this. Why can we not allow a husband and wife team to arrange their income for taxation purposes to their best advantage? For the most part they do not do this. A husband and wife operating a small business do not have the finances to hire the best accountants and lawyers to look after their situation as do large corporations which have full-time staffs of tax consultants. We are trying to close a small loophole. It is as though there were something wicked about a married couple arranging their affairs to pay the least possible tax.
We can only assume that this government is trying to encourage immorality. If two people who are not married decide to live together under the same roof, they are able to arrange their affairs. One can work for the other. In this situation, they could arrange the best tax advantage. A taxation law such as this encourages immorality.
Hear, hear!

This important concept should be discussed and amended. Our party will propose an amendment in this regard. I hope the amendment will be accepted. It may not be acceptable to this government, but I know it will be acceptable to the people of Canada.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The opposition always stands for morality.
Income Tax Act

We should be considering taxation policies that will encourage and increase the Canadian businessmen, not take away their piddling incomes and make them all slaves of the state. We should encourage small business. In the majority of small businesses, farms for example, the wife works side by side with her husband 16 hours per day year in and year out. Sometimes they work for 20 or 30 years without even a holiday until they retire. This is the loophole which the government is trying to close. The government says it wants to make them equitable, on a tax basis, with the employee. This is what they are doing. The man and wife team working 16 hours per day, bucking the prairie wind or operating a small grocery store from 8 a.m. until midnight, are the people who will be affected by section 75. I will not go any further at this point because we will be moving an amendment in order to try to rectify this situation.

Mr. Chairman, the amendment which will be moved shortly by the hon. member for Edmonton West has just been drafted. It might be called something that was inspired by the ill-considered intervention, not in debate but outside this House, of the chief government whip, the member for Vancouver Quadra. I always felt that if you had something you really wanted to pursue vigorously, you should have the guts to stand up and face your peers in the House of Commons and not do it by the backdoor route of assassination, the back alley route to the parliamentary press gallery.
If the Prime Minister and other top people on the government side ask what, for heaven's sake, went wrong in the House of Commons on a Friday afternoon, when all was supposed to be sweetness and good housekeeping on the provisions of the Income Tax Act which have existed for many years, they will get the answer from the chief government whip, "Mea culpa". It is a villainous attack on Members of Parliament in very serious deliberation to use the route which he did.
Some members, including myself, have questioned the method we are using to bring about tax reform in this country. At least it can be said to our credit that we are here sweating, struggling and straining while working on very complex and tough issues. We are trying to do it in a spirit of exchange with the parliamentary secretary. At least there is dialogue, however imperfect, in the people's forum. That is important. For the chief government whip to issue his attack upon all of us and our methods, which can only denigrate Parliament, it is a great disservice to this institution.
That comment having been made, I want to reinforce what I said previously about the portion of the act we are dealing with and the amendment that will be moved by the hon. member for Edmonton West. The problem we are dealing with is large to people with a very small income, it is of no consequence to people who have no problems in this world. This problem really concerns people whose joint income is below $3,650 a year. In this area it does not pay people to incorporate. By that simple action they will lose approximately $500. What advantages will flow from it in the long run?
We are dealing with two people with an income of less than $3,650 a year. They may be operating a small grocery store, a mamma and papa garage or a mamma and papa

November 5, 1971
Income Tax Act
boutique. If we cannot look after people like that we must consider our attempts in the field of tax reform to be unworthy. We are certainly going to do something for mining companies and for the "big guys". But if we cannot deal with two people who are trying to be good Canadians and raise a family on a small income, then none of us deserves to come back here. Accordingly, the hon. member for Edmonton West has written out his amendment and it will be presented as soon as Your Honour sees fit to recognize it.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make a brief commentary on this section since I find it a very unsetting one. This is in keeping with the theme of Liberal government policy for the past 31 years, namely to wipe out small entities to destroy family units. Certainly that is happening under this provision. I want the parliamentary secretary to explain why it is such a big sin for a husband to want to employ his wife in a small business and be so heavily penalized by our taxation laws.
A similar situation prevails with a husband and wife who set up a small company and she is a partner in the company, not an employee. Why should they be penalized by the provision that the income of the company is considered the income of one person? I think both of these provisions are destructive of the family unit, of family businesses such as small farms, corner stores, and so on. This kind of provision should be amended in order to promote small business.
We all know very well that most of the job opportunities in this country are provided not only by the huge corporations, which the government put forward as examples of the nth degree of efficiency; we must also realize that in the long run the family farm and the family business is still the backbone of society and the way its people earn their living. When we bracket sections such as this with the estate tax proposal of a year or two ago we see at once almost no hope for the family business to survive and to be passed on to the heirs and successors. It is a very bad principle to destroy units of this sort.
I think it is fair to say that many of the people who came to Canada during the last 50 or 100 years did so in the knowledge that in this country any individual with initiative should be able without too much difficulty to establish and to run successfully a business or a farming operation of his own. In view of this we must not allow this kind of destructive legislation to go forward.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not want to delay the well heralded amendment that is coming from my hon. friend for Edmonton West, but perhaps he would be grateful for another moment or two in which to draft it.
No, I have it ready.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
In any case, some of the things that have been said during the last half hour prompt me to get briefly to my feet. I know some of the conditions that have been described by my hon. friends to my right do exist; there are cases where married couples have to work all kinds of hours to maintain their livelihood. Some of the stories have been pretty

heart-rending. Some people work 16 hours a day almost every day of the week and go 20 years without a holiday. I do not deny that this happens, but I suggest that these situations call for far more than simply adjustments in income tax; they call for a guaranteed annual income, for other means of recognizing the sanctity of family life in this country than simply acknowledging that it is all right for people to slave like this if they get an income tax adjustment. I hope that the government will respond to the arguments that have been presented this afternoon in a far more positive way than simply changing the Income Tax Act, important as that may be.

Mr. Chairman, notwithstanding the fact that the other day we passed a subsection (6) which included a subparagraph (viii) which is related to section 74, the really operative clause dealing with this situation is the one before us. Subsection (3) provides:
Where a person has received remuneration as an employee of his spouse-
I suppose the masculine includes the feminine in the interpretation of statutes.
-the amount thereof shall not be deducted in computing the spouse's income and shall not be included in computing the employee's income.
Then subsection (5) provides:
Where a husband and wife were partners in a business, the income of one spouse from the business for a taxation year may, in the discretion of the minister, be deemed to belong to the other spouse.
We have the same principle here, though in the second instance this is discretionary. It will be interesting to see what criteria will be used by the minister to lump, within his discretion, the income of the two into the pocket of the one. I suppose there was a time when it was felt when this was income splitting and that there would be a reduction in the marginal rates; but it seems to me that this is secondary to the principle that we must now recognize, that we are in a different age. We now have far more women working. If women are working for their husbands, as I have pointed out and as I shall continue to point out ad nauseam if need be, if the husband is the principal owner of a limited company the wife can claim workers allowance or child care allowance in an appropriate case. She is also covered by unemployment insurance and comes within the Canada Pension Plan.
However, as long as such spouses are covered by section 74(3), and discretionarily so under section 74(5), they are not able to avail themselves of workers allowance and child care allowance and are not covered under the Canada Pension Plan or eligible for unemployment insurance. Therefore, it seems to me that since we are trying to urge women to work, including married women, they should not suffer from this disability.
Someone was talking about encouraging immorality. Certainly a man could pay his mistress to work for him, in which case she would get the advantage of child care allowance, workers allowance, and qualify for the Canada Pension Plan and unemployment insurance. Her husband doing the same work should be entitled to the same benefits, but in fact he is not entitled to any of them. This might be a very favourable incentive to men to take up
November 5, 1971

that type of casual relationship. In this way they could avail themselves of these benefits under the Income Tax Act.
We know there are other sections that define an illegitimate child as a child within the meaning of the act. There are all sorts of provisions in the act which remove what formerly were moral bars. If you adopt that stand in spite of those positions, then I must say you cannot now impose an artificial provision in respect of a husband and his spouse. For that reason I would move:
That section 74 be amended by deleting therefrom subsections (3) and (5), and renumbering subsection (4) in consequence thereto.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. Hon. members have heard the motion moved by the hon. member for Edmonton West. Without accepting the motion procedurally, I invite hon. members to assist the Chair on the procedural aspect. I am sure the hon. member for Edmonton West and others will help me in this regard. I have some concern in respect of the deletion of two subsections in that this would change or shift the incidence of taxation. That is a preliminary thought but I ask hon. members to assist me if they wish.

I have a little difficulty following the views of the Chair, in that amendments from both sides of the House have been accepted and denied although many of them have had the same effect; they have disturbed the balance of ways and means. An amendment accepted by Your Honour the other day, moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, as well as one moved by the hon. member for Regina East, certainly disturbed the balance of ways and means; however, they were accepted.
This amendment does not pick on any particular class of taxpayer. It merely deletes certain subsections of this section which relate to separate taxes for spouses, either male or female. The wording of the section is that a person receiving remuneration as an employee of a spouse is entitled to certain things. This does not exclusively relate to a wife who receives remuneration from her husband; it also involves a husband who receives remuneration from his wife. A hotel business owned by a wife, of which the husband is an employee, should fall into this category. Unless the hotel is incorporated, the husband's salary is treated as part of the income of the wife. Therefore there is no more benefit to a so-called shareholder. All we are attempting to do is remove this discrimination. One person is an employee and the other is the employer. Either one could be the spouse and this is true in respect of a husband and wife operating as partners.
It seems to me that my amendment does not disturb ways and means to a greater extent than the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre which the Chair accepted. The same is true of the motion put forward by the hon. member for Regina East. All I can say is that those two amendments were acceptable. I am not using them as examples and I am not taking into account any specific class of taxpayer. All I am saying is that people should be treated as individuals. Whether they are married or not should not have a bearing on the fact that they
Income Tax Act
are to be treated as individuals. Keeping in mind the Chair has accepted other amendments of this kind in the course of this debate, I suggest my amendment is in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I direct one point to the hon. member's attention and I do so in order to indicate my concern in this matter. My concern is not directed to a disturbance of ways and means. I make this comment so hon. members can direct their remarks to it. My concern is related to the fact that a private member cannot do something which can only be done by the Crown.
There is a citation in Beauchesne which would appear to be the authority for a private member to move to reduce taxes. The view I have taken throughout this debate is that while such a motion is in order, it must be an across-the-board reduction and it cannot shift the burden of taxation from one taxpayer to another. That is the consistent view I have taken on other occasions when I have made rulings. It seems to me that if subections (3) and (5) are deleted, one taxpayer or another will pay more or less. That is my real concern.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, anticipating that you might say what you have said, I prepared a few remarks on this point of order. Let us consider subsection (5) first, in light of the fact that there may not be any alteration at all, or a shifting of tax burden, we must consider the amendment on its own merits. We must assume that the minister is concerned and that the Chair is governed by a principle of equity. That being so, we must assume that only the minister in exercising his discretion will make a change shifting the incidence of taxation. I think there is no arithmetical means of deciding now whether there is likely to be or will be any shift in the incidence of taxation, particularly with regard to subsection (5). The subec-tion provides:
-the income of one spouse from the business for a taxation year may, in the discretion of the minister, be deemed to belong to the other spouse.
The word "may" is permissive. I would suggest, therefore, that the hon. member for Edmonton West is just taking away that permissive discretion which is otherwise granted to the minister. There is no firm means of determining there is any shift in the incidence. It is only a very slight walk to take us to subection (3). Is it not within the realm of possibility, or what we consider to be possibility-because there is not before the Chair any means by which to determine precisely what is going to be the change-that a husband and wife, working together in the circumstances which have been so eloquently portrayed by my hon. friends, could in fact create a larger income? There might be no shift at all.
These are all possibilities which we are examining here. May I say, with respect, that I challenge the Chair or anyone else to look at those two subsections and say there will be, there can be or is likely to be any shift in the incidence of taxation. It remains a possibility, but only a possibility. I say to the Chair that I believe the standard rule is that if the Chair approaches a question of the propriety of any motion and whether or not it is in order, then the onus falls upon those who say it is not in order-

November 5, 1971
Income Tax Act
and if Your Honour has any doubt I suggest it must be resolved in favour of the propriety of the motion.

Due to the invitation of Your Honour to address myself to the question of shifting the incidence of tax, I would point out that this problem has been debated to a considerable extent in the past and in no case more extensively than on the basis of an amendment I moved when a bill was being considered arising out of the budget of 1970. The government at that time was proposing a 5 per cent excise tax on airline tickets. I proposed an amendment that would not change the balance of ways and means. With the greatest respect, I would put to the Chair that the question of balance of ways and means is the operative point and that the incidence of tax is of no consequence.
My motion finally was ruled out, based upon a citation in May's sevententh edition. I researched the citation and found that the editors of May's misreported the case, giving it a completely reverse meaning to what was the result. This meaning had been inferred from a decision of the chairman of the committee of the whole in the British House during World War I on a matter that was not debated. This is the sole citation that was used against the principle I invoked so far as the incidence of taxation is concerned.
No question has been raised concerning the balance of ways and means, but a decision of Your Honour has been given on two occasions accepting amendments which disturb the balance of ways and means. I will admit this does disturb the balance of ways and means, but so far as the question of incidence is concerned I say simply that the disability with regard to certain taxpayers will be removed and they will be treated as individuals. There will be no forceful pairing.
Under the circumstances I would invite Your Honour, now that it is four o'clock, to look at the judgment of His Honour Mr. Speaker in regard to the incidence of tax and the arguments I advanced on that occasion, basing myself on May's authority and the subsequent correspondence which ensued between the Clerk of the House and the editors of May's because I called into question the authorities that were cited against me.
I would call it four o'clock, Mr. Chairman.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, November 9, 1970, consideration of the motion of Mr. McGrath (St. John's East):
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to protect the privacy of every person against the improper disclosure of credit rating records and to protect the reputation of every person against misinformation contained in such records.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MEASURE TO PROTECT PRIVACY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are resuming debate on a motion that was brought forward by my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), almost a year ago to the day, on November 9, 1970, and because of the length of this session we again have an opportunity to debate it.
Before moving into the main body of my address I would like to point out that once again in private members' hour we are dealing with a motion that was supported by all parties a year ago, and the fact that action has not been taken on it indicates we have not resolved a substantial problem connected with private members' hour. On the previous occasion there was almost unanimous agreement that the motion be passed, yet simply because there is no machinery in many cases to move motions beyond debate in private members' hour this motion has remained on the order paper for a year.
I hope that during the interim the government House leader and others in the cabinet have had a chance to study this very reasonable motion with a view to having the substance of it referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs where it could be more adequately dealt with than in this House.
In this debate we are dealing with the matter of credit ratings and the way in which they are used. Credit ratings are used not only to assess the nature of one's ability to pay one's debts but also to assess one's honesty and dependability as an individual. That affects jobs, promotions, appointments and the like. In essence, it affects the right of decent individuals to advance within a free society. We are wondering what response there will be from the government to take account of the rapid accumulation of information in credit card ratings, which is often best
November 5, 1971

described as misinformation, containing typographical errors and irresponsible judgments.
To give an example, Mr. Speaker, just a few weeks ago I was phoned by a credit bureau with regard to an account that was outstanding and as the bureau employee spoke I told him that I would be interested in knowing what kind of information they had on my card. He began to tell me that once I had a telephone bill that I had not paid, in a town where I was working for a national chain store. I told him that was all very interesting, except that I have never been employed by any national chain store and had never had a phone bill in the place he mentioned. He became a bit embarassed and said, "Maybe we had better check back on some of this." I suddenly realized what it is to have misinformation accumulated in a file where it could be used against me any time in the future.
This motion deals specifically with the credit bureau rating systems and generally with the individual's right to privacy within our society. For over 200 years the courts have established that one of the fundamental principles of common law is that nobody, be he a state official or not, is empowered to enter on our personal property. Some provinces are now attempting to legislate in this area, and this points up the need to have some common standard.
We also have a long tradition that people are considered innocent until proven guilty. Yet the accumulation of credit information in this country has given rise to a situation in which a person can be found guilty without his knowledge, and as a consequence steps may be taken detrimental to him by those who otherwise might employ him, offer him credit or transact some other form of business with him.
Unless we apply stringent safeguards in our contemporary society we are in danger of losing the fundamental rights of privacy and property. Modern devices such as wire tapping, highly sophisticated microphones, cameras for surveillance and the establishment of computer data banks and processing centres must be controlled. If not controlled they can easily become the instruments of suppression and totalitarianism.
I realize that credit records are but one small sector of the larger question of privacy in the face of modern technology. However, the dissemination of credit information is one measure of the problem and is an area in which we can start to build a good system of checks and balances which will stipulate in law that uncontrolled and improper collection and the haphazard storage and distribution of confidential records, many of which are sold for commercial gain, will not be allowed, and in particular that the accumulation of inaccurate and hearsay information will definitely be counteracted by the individual's right to know and his right to clear away this kind of misinformation from the files.
As in all areas of technology, the pace of input into and output from any system is obviously going to be improved by innovation. Soon credit information will be computerized or microfilmed. The result will be a quantum increase in the availability of this information to those who might benefit from it. Finance agencies with quicker recall and improved facilities may find it advantageous to record the lives of customers in greater detail.
Protection of Privacy of Credit Records
The whole trend of modern technology clearly underlines the need for greater government involvement. It is all too obvious that a good deal of the information that goes into these files has nothing to do with the individual's ability to transact his business or handle his commercial affairs but can easily involve a lot of other affairs that are no part of the information on one's credit rating. The need for clear government regulations to cover collection agencies, their operation and the rating of the individual between federal and provincial governments is obvious.
It is a truism to say that massive credit is here to stay. Consumerism has obviously been built and made vital to the operation of the marketplace. Outstanding consumer credit in this country totalled $9.4 billion at the end of August, 1971, which over a three-month period represents a 3.8 per cent increase. For better or worse we are heavily entrenched in the wonderful world of credit.
I should like to outline some of the inner workings of a credit bureau. Most of them have automated file systems that are not computerized as yet. Their credit cards are retroactive to November, 1964, or for about seven years. Cards at a minimum contain court judgments, writs, bankruptcies, foreclosures, collections, marital status, general credit rating and such things as chattel mortgages, etc. At a maximum, according to the Canadian Association of Consumers, they include salaries, wages, resume on domestic life and even personality outlines. At the moment there is no standardized way of reporting credit profiles in Canada.
In Ontario, standard procedure when a member business of a credit bureau calls to check on an individual's credit is to simply read down that individual's credit card outlining derogatory information such as collections, etc., which have been marked in red pencil. In other words, they simply go down a list covering seven years and in some cases dating back 14 years. The decision to grant credit or not is arbitrarily decided by the member calling for the information. And, as it is well known, once an individual is tagged as having an overloaded credit rating it often affects not only further business transactions by the individual but also that person's chances of further employment or promotion in the community.
According to the statement of policy to ensure the right of privacy to consumers released by the Associated Credit Bureaux of Canada in 1970, "Credit bureaux will make known to any consumer their file content concerning that consumer." The flaw here is that the code is voluntary and a large proportion of credit bureaux do not belong to this organization. In many cases the individuals most affected by this improper information or misuse of information are so intimidated or so unaware of their rights that advantage can be taken of them. Last year, the Canadian Association of Consumers undertook in its own words, a nationwide survey of credit bureau attitudes and found that many credit bureaux are still reluctant to show files even if the person has recently been refused credit.
Because inadequacies still exist in the use of credit ratings, and the risk to individuals who are affected by them is still great, we are calling for realistic legislation and enforcement in this area believing it is the responsibility of the federal government to take this initiative. At
9396

November 5, 1971
Protection of Privacy of Credit Records
present there exists in Canada no legislative regulation of data processing at the national level. Our party advocates controls to ensure that the privacy and reputations of Canadians are protected. In particular, all companies which collect information and dispense ratings and personal information on Canadian consumers which operate within federal jurisdiction should require a government operating licence and operate according to provincial standards.
The possible influence of companies with large amounts of economic, social and even political information on individuals is sinister. We strongly advocate the establishment of government studies and regulations relating to data collecting which, done in conjunction with the provinces, would set specified standards for the protection of the individual's rights and privacy.
In general I should like to give an illustration of the regulations that we might have so that the consumer would have rights under the law. These might be: first, that the consumer be told the name and address of the credit agency when he is denied credit, insurance or employment and it should be done at the time that he is refused; second, the consumer should be able to examine information in his file at the credit agency when credit action is taken against him; third, he should be told the sources of information in his file and to whom such information has been given; fourth, such data should be confidential, except for legitimate purposes such as a credit reference or job; fifth, disputed information should be reinvestigated with false data deleted, and notification of deletion sent to those who received erroneous reports within a specified period of time.
Sixth, he should be informed of investigations involving interviews with other persons about his personal life and have the right to be informed on the kind of questions which were being asked; seventh, he should be informed when adverse public record information is reported to a potential employer; eight, he should, after having access to record cards or a computer print-out, be able to bring legal action against those companies which do not comply with government regulations.
There have been some encouraging signs of governments coming to grips with this issue, most recently the province of Ontario. However, the federal government, which at very least should encourage guidelines to coordinate national standards for credit data organizations, has done very little in this field. The flow of detailed information is vital to the functioning of our modern society. However, the regulation and control of that information, when it affects an individual's livelihood, is equally important to the preservation of the individual's right to privacy in which we all so strongly believe.
Credit ratings are more than just optional measurements by which the honest gain and the dishonest are harmed. In a society that is increasingly based upon one's ability to have credit awarded or assessed, the credit rating is almost a matter of integrity, both financial and otherwise. It is disturbing that so little action has been taken federally on this important subject. I would hope when we are dealing with something as basic as the establishment of credit that we would feel it proper and necessary to take action on this matter as early as possible.

I would therefore like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Peddle):
That the subject matter of the motion now before the House be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
I believe in committee this matter should receive more detailed and adequate consideration for the formulation of effective federal legislation.
