Mr. Speaker, the thought has occurred to me that in view of the suggestion which has been made, while I am making my remarks the consultation suggested might take place. I would not object if there were those discussions. I agree that the subject matter of the motion is most important. It is worthy of consideration by hon. members of this House and I think that giving those concerned an opportunity to appear before the standing committee might be a most useful exercise.
The hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) obviously had a well prepared representation to make on the subject matter before the House as well as on related subject matters. If I remember correctly, he listed eight or nine points which he felt should be considered. I listened carefully to the hon. member and for the most part I agree with his suggestion. I am sure no one would quarrel with the idea that it is necessary for people who are operating businesses to have some basis on which to assess whether credit should be extended to an individual customer.
I suppose it is true to say, as the hon. member for Egmont suggested, that we will live in a society where a large volume of business will be transacted either on a long-term or short-term credit basis. Yet most of us in the course of our lives have observed occasions when knowledge, acquired through mechanisms developed in the business world for accumulating and recording information relating to credit ratings, is abused. Since the credit system is so firmly established and is in such wide use, I think some ground rules in law ought to be laid down for the governing of such operations.
One of the things that concerns me greatly-and I speak as one who has had experience of other people who have been involved in difficulties in this regard-is that no one seems to know just who has what information about us. I do not know how many credit bureaux have me listed on credit cards somewhere, either in Ottawa, British Columbia or in some other part of the country. There may be information about me tucked away in some central recording centre in Toronto for all I know.
As a matter of protection to the individual it should be defined that anyone holding such information must advise the person about whom they hold the information and, indeed, they should have to advise them what information they have. This in itself would provide protection to the individual against the recording and perpetuation of incorrect information about a particular individual. Perhaps it would do something to straighten out the circumstances that occur fairly frequently with regard to mistaken identity where the information that is presumably recorded about one individual relates to and is connected with another. This is one of the basics that should be required by law for all those who are involved in the operation and accumulation of credit information.
There has been a good deal of talk about the fact that we live in an acquisitive society. Perhaps a new term should be applied and it should now be called an inquisi-

tive society. For example, having been a customer of the B.C. Telephone Company for a good many years I recently had occasion to make application for the installation of a new telephone in another location. I was faced with the current application form which asked all manner of questions about me, my employer and various other things. Apparently it wanted some sort of guarantor. It struck me that this was going a bit far on the part of one of the public utilities in this country. The matter of who you work for really does not have anything to do with the B.C. Telephone Company installing a telephone in your residence.
I think that kind of inquisitiveness should be restrained by law, particularly by a telephone company which collects their charges in advance each month. I have no way of knowing to what organizations the B.C. Telephone Company may belong. I do not know how much of the information they acquire as a result of people making applications for telephones is passed on to other, unknown destinations. This is the sort of thing that is of increasing concern to more and more individuals.
As pointed out earlier in the discussion, this situation becomes rather frightening and horrifying with the advent of the computer. From time to time we have the feeling that we are going to simply become numbers or some sort of code on a tape and cease to have any identity as an individual, living human being. Apart from anything else, it might help to preserve the sense of human freedom and identity if citizens know that there are some legal ground rules laid down to govern the operation of recording and using information on which credit decisions can be based.

Reports cannot gather dust until they are finished and tabled. It is probably in the process of being written, so it cannot be gathering dust yet. As things go around here, dust does not settle very quickly but seems to stay up in the air most of the time, especially at this stage of the session.
As several of my colleagues have said, the problem of unregulated gathering of credit information can certainly be abused drastically in this computer age. Mastering knowledge has been aided by computers. Computers can master knowledge and use it to the detriment of individuals. This could not be done in former days because of the sheer mass of knowledge. I note that Dr. John Deutsch, chairman of a panel at a conference entitled "Computers,
Protection of Privacy of Credit Records
Privacy and Freedom of Information" held in May, 1970, put this quite succinctly. If I may quote from page 42 of "Instant World, a Report on Telecommunications in Canada", he said:
In the past, we've had a protection from the limitations of the written word. While a lot of information could be collected, it was cumbersome, it was difficult to find, certainly difficult to find quickly, and this has given the individual a good deal of protection as far as privacy is concerned. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack. Well, what's happened now is that we can indeed find the needle.
That is the nub of the threat that computers pose to mankind. They can be a wonderful servant but they can also find needles that they have no business to find, revealing information that used to be buried by the normal course of events.
The ease of collecting and disseminating credit information, thanks to the computer, brings to light a number of new problem areas. First of all, there is incorrect information which can be propagated and disseminated without disclosing the source of the information or anyone being able to check the information. Then there is misuse of information. For example, information on credit ratings could be misused by those directly related to the gathering of the information or by those who come across information in computer handling.
Last year my colleague the hon. member for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault) mentioned in his intervention on this motion that he had been closely associated with a large insurance company during his career. As reported at page 1020 of Hansard for November 9, 1970, he said:
I have had the opportunity to look at credit reports and I have often noticed, with disgust, that some of those credit reports contained information which had nothing to do with the financial situation of the persons involved.
Then he went on to say it was-
-information which has absolutely nothing to do with the financial situation, the steadiness and solvency of the individual involved.
So you can see that the information may have nothing to do with the inquiry that is made. That is bad enough, but when compounded by computer technology the problem is even worse. I presume the hon. member was referring to pre-computer days and the sort of reports that those of us who work in offices have often seen floating around. When this is added to the fact we are now in the computer age, you can see we really have a problem as far as the average individual is concerned. A person may be aware of various fragments of information that has been gathered by different sources. He may not be perturbed about these little bits and pieces of information that various people have on him; but if all these bits and pieces are gathered together by a computer a very extensive personal dossier could be compiled without his knowing it. He could be completely unaware of such a dossier and its contents.
Because the computer industry has grown so quickly and is still in a state of flux, I see no hope on the horizon for a self-regulating body that one could look to to police the industry and to cure some of its ills. Therefore, it is only right and fitting that motions of the sort we are discussing today should be moved and that the govern-

November 5, 1971
Protection of Privacy of Credit Records
ment should take the action that it is now in the full process of taking. After all, there is a real problem here.
I should like to think that when we consider both the present motion and the actions that the government is putting together as a package, we consider also the following recommendations very seriously. First of all, the licensing of data banks which would gather, store and disseminate this kind of information; second, that regulation of the sale and disposal of information stored in these banks be made mandatory; third, that regulation of international links between data banks be built into the industry. We would then know exactly what information is leaving Canada and what is coming into Canada. I think every Canadian is horrified that sooner or later the ultimate will arrive and in a little basement in an office in New York every scrap of information on every single person in Canada will be available. Certainly this would be a poor state of affairs.
I have other comments to make, Mr. Speaker, but it is five o'clock and I am afraid I will not be allowed to go on unless the House allows me a little longer.
